ui.compare.title: Your choices and Fux's, weighed
ui.compare.intro: Where your notes and Fux's differ, a criterion Fux himself states sometimes favours one of them; only those places are listed.
ui.compare.none: Your counterpoint is identical to Fux's.
ui.compare.fuxBetter.imperfect: Fux's imperfect consonance serves his rule of more imperfect than perfect consonances (p. 46).
ui.compare.playerBetter.imperfect: Your imperfect consonance serves that rule (p. 46) better than Fux's perfect one here.
ui.compare.fuxBetter.motion: Fux arrives here by contrary or oblique motion, which he recommends (p. 45); you arrive by similar motion.
ui.compare.playerBetter.motion: You arrive here by contrary or oblique motion (p. 45); Fux arrives by similar motion.
ui.compare.fuxBetter.singable: Fux's line moves by smaller intervals there, so it is easier to sing (p. 53: everything in counterpoint should be very easy to sing).
ui.compare.playerBetter.singable: Your line moves by smaller intervals there, so it is easier to sing (p. 53).
ui.compare.equal: By Fux's stated criteria the two choices are equally good here; the difference is one of taste or of the line as a whole.
ui.compare.mann.player: Mann would have scored yours higher:
ui.compare.mann.fux: Mann would have scored Fux's higher:
ui.compare.mann.largeLeap: no leap larger than a fifth (the octave and the rising minor sixth excepted)
ui.compare.mann.leapsSameWay: no two leaps in the same direction
ui.compare.mann.uncompensated: a leap answered by motion the other way
ui.compare.mann.repeatedTwice: no tone repeated more than once
ui.compare.mannNote: Lines marked "Mann" apply Alfred Mann's melodic advice from the footnotes of his translation (1965, pp. 27 and 29): his, not Fux's.
ui.compare.taste: Where you differ from Fux, no criterion he states favours either choice: the differences are matters of taste.

ui.withFux.title: With Fux
ui.withFux.help: Your line, Fux's line and the cantus sung together: how close you came to him, and how the two lines sound as three-voice counterpoint.
ui.withFux.badgeHelp: Share of your notes that are Fux's own, note for note and in the same place ({same} of {n}).
ui.withFux.identical: Your line is Fux's own, note for note. Did you do it by yourself?!
ui.withFux.close: {pct}% of your notes are Fux's own ({same} of {n}): you and Josephus walked almost the same road.
ui.withFux.remarkable: Only {pct}% of your notes are Fux's, and yet the two lines sound together with the cantus without a single fault: an independent counterpoint that would also make a clean trio. Remarkable work — Josephus would have been proud of that.
ui.withFux.good: Your line goes its own way (only {pct}% of its notes are Fux's), and it is good counterpoint against his too: the three voices are clean in {clean} of {n} places.
ui.withFux.uneven: Your line goes its own way ({pct}% of its notes are Fux's), and as a trio it is uneven: the three voices are clean in {clean} of {n} places, and fault in the rest.
ui.withFux.clash: Your line goes its own way ({pct}% of its notes are Fux's) and the two clash: sung together with the cantus they make faulty counterpoint in {bad} of {n} places. That says nothing against your line on its own, which is judged above — only that the two solutions do not live together.
ui.withFux.locked: Clear this exercise to compare your line with Fux's.
ui.withFux.incomplete: Fill every place to compare your line with Fux's.
ui.trio.intro: Sung together, the two counterpoints and the cantus make a three-voice texture. Each line against the cantus has been judged above; this reads what the third voice adds. Bars are numbered from 1.
ui.trio.introHalf: Sung together, the two counterpoints and the cantus make a three-voice texture. Each line against the cantus has been judged above; this reads what the third voice adds. Positions: bar number, a = downbeat, b = upbeat.
ui.trio.noFaults: No clash and no forbidden succession between your line and Fux's.
ui.trio.dissonanceWithBass: {where}: your line and Fux's make a dissonance ({detail}) against the lowest voice.
ui.trio.dissonanceBetweenUppers: {where}: your line and Fux's clash ({detail}) above the cantus (between upper voices only the fourth passes).
ui.trio.parallelPerfect: {where}: parallel {detail} between your line and Fux's.
ui.trio.directPerfectOuter: {where}: the outer voices (your line and Fux's) move in similar motion into a {detail}.
ui.trio.unison: {where}: your line and Fux's meet in unison; the texture thins to two voices there.
ui.trio.completeTriad: Complete harmony (three different notes, all consonant) in {n} places: {where}.
ui.trio.contrary: Your line and Fux's move in contrary motion in {n} places: {where}.

ui.species.third: Third species: four quarter notes against one

ui.export.help: Save what plays now, with every setting, as an audio file (MP3 or WAV)
ui.export.intro: The game plays the piece and records exactly what you hear (voices, versions, drums, continuo, tempo), then saves it as a file. Recording runs in real time; keep this tab open.
ui.export.kindQuestion: Mix mode? In mix mode you set up several loops, each its own way, and they are exported one after another as one continuous piece.
ui.export.kind.single.help: record what is set up now, for one or more passes (you can still mix live while it records)
ui.export.kind.mix.help: a different setup for each loop: sounds and mix, versions, your line, drums, continuo, tempo, which lines play
ui.export.mixHow: A bar at the bottom of the page then takes you through the loops: set up loop 1 (play it to hear it), press › for loop 2, and so on; a new loop starts as a copy of the one before. When they are ready, press Export.
ui.export.mixIntro: The {n} loops play one after another, each with its own setup, and are saved as one file. Recording runs in real time; keep this tab open.
ui.export.mixSetUp: set up this loop as you want it heard, then ›
ui.export.mixEditing: this loop is set up; change it, or move on
ui.export.mixPlaying: the loops play as you set them up
ui.export.ending.seamless.help: Cut exactly where the next pass would begin, so the file loops seamlessly in a player
ui.export.ending.final.help: The last pass ends as the piece ends: the drums' final stroke and the reverb's tail
ui.export.live: You can mix while it records: faders, balance, mute and solo, sounds, versions, drums, continuo and tempo all go into the file as you change them. Stop and save at any time.
ui.export.mixLive: mix live: every change is recorded
ui.export.mp3: recommended: small (about 1.4 MB a minute), plays everywhere, sends on WhatsApp as audio. On claude.ai it comes inside a .zip.
ui.export.wav: lossless, for editing elsewhere; about ten times larger
ui.export.zipped: {format} saved, inside a .zip (this viewer saves only some file types): unzip it to get the audio.
ui.export.failed: The audio could not be recorded in this browser.

ui.drums.resetLoop: Back to this pattern's own length ({n})
ui.drums.loopHelp: How long one loop of the pattern lasts. The arrows go ¼, ⅓, ½, ⅔, ¾ bar, then 1, 2, 4 and 8 bars, then 3, 5 and 6, then the polymetric lengths: 3 loops in 4 bars, 2 in 3, 4 in 5, 3 in 5, 5 in 8, 3 in 8 — the pattern turning against the bar. Click the length to go back to the preset's own.
ui.drums.boxHelp: Choose a kit, then one of its presets (★ the kit's paradigm); either starts from the preset's defaults.
ui.drums.kit.studio.help: The game's own synthesized drum kit, for rock, funk and the like.
ui.drums.kit.tr808.help: After the Roland TR-808 (1980), all analog: a long, booming bass drum, a hissing snare, the metallic hats and the two-tone cowbell. Synthesized here, not sampled.
ui.drums.kit.tr909.help: After the Roland TR-909 (1983): a punchy swept bass drum, a bright snare and clap. Its cymbals were 6-bit samples on the original; here they are imitated.
ui.drums.kit.cr78.help: After the Roland CR-78 CompuRhythm (1978): soft, small analog voices, the ticking metal beat, tambourine and guiro.
ui.drums.kit.rhythmAce.help: After the Ace Tone Rhythm Ace (1967) and the preset rhythm boxes of the organ era: short, dull, plain sounds.
ui.drums.kit.sdsv.help: After the Simmons SDS-V (1981): toms and snare with a deep downward pitch bend.
ui.drums.pattern.electro.help: An early-80s electro groove on the 808: syncopated bass drum, clap, cowbell, conga.
ui.drums.pattern.slowjam.help: A soul ballad groove on the 808, with rim clicks and a low conga.
ui.drums.pattern.house.help: Four on the floor on the 909: clap on two and four, open hats on the off-beats.
ui.drums.pattern.techno.help: Techno on the 909, written over two bars: a deep four-on-the-floor, an off-beat open hat, accented sixteenth hats, the clap on the backbeat, a shifting rim figure and a ride that swells at the end.
ui.drums.pattern.newwave.help: A late-70s CR-78 pattern: soft kick and snare, ticking hats, tambourine and guiro.
ui.drums.pattern.rhythmbox.help: A preset-style beat from an organ-era rhythm box: kick, snare, claves and cymbal.
ui.drums.pattern.synthtoms.help: An 80s pattern on Simmons drums, with falling-pitch tom fills.
ui.drums.pattern.rock.help: Kick, backbeat snare and eighth-note hi-hat.
ui.drums.pattern.funk.help: Syncopated kick, ghost notes on the snare, sixteenth hats.
ui.drums.pattern.halftime.help: A heavy groove with the snare on the third beat, and a ride cymbal.
ui.drums.pattern.bossa.help: Rim clicks, soft kick and shaker.
ui.drums.pattern.conga.help: Congas over a cowbell bell pattern and a shaker.
ui.drums.pattern.clave.help: Son clave on claves, woodblock and bongos.
ui.drums.pattern.tribal.help: Djembe bass and slaps, frame drum and shaker.
ui.drums.pattern.taiko.help: Big drums, rim clicks and claps.
ui.drums.pattern.ritual.help: A slow heartbeat on the frame drum, with a triangle.
ui.drums.pattern.timpani.help: Timpani on the final and the fifth; a roll before the last bar, cymbals at the end.
ui.drums.pattern.march.help: Field drum, bass drum, cymbals and a timpano.
ui.drums.pattern.processional.help: Bass drum, soft timpani and a triangle.
ui.drums.tap.help: Tap tempo: tap two or more times in time with the half notes (the beat of the cantus) and the tempo follows.
ui.drums.swing.help: Swing delays every second sixteenth, as on the MPC and the vintage machines: 50% is straight, 66% is a triplet shuffle. Shuffle patterns written in triplets are not swung further.
ui.drums.accent.help: Accent: the accented steps of the pattern louder and the others softer, like the accent of the TR-808 and its kin.
ui.drums.variation.help: Variation A (the pattern), B (a busier version of it), or A and B alternating loop by loop.
ui.drums.autoFill.help: Auto fill: a fill at the end of every pass of the loop (and, without the loop, in the bar before the last). Off, the groove runs straight through.
ui.drums.pads.help: The kit's nine pads light up as the pattern plays. Click a pad to step through what it plays: as the preset has it, other parts written for that instrument (cowbell on the downbeats, the off-beats, a clave…), and off. A pad the preset leaves silent starts at off.
ui.drums.cue.fill1.help: The pattern's own fill, at the end of the bar that is playing (heard at once when nothing plays).
ui.drums.cue.fill2.help: A snare roll that grows louder, at the end of the bar that is playing.
ui.drums.cue.fill3.help: Down the toms, at the end of the bar that is playing.
ui.drums.cue.fill4.help: Stop-time: three hits across the bar with the snare and bass drum together, then back in.
ui.drums.cue.break.help: A one-bar break: a hit on the downbeat, then silence until the next bar, where the groove returns on a crash.
ui.drums.kit.sixties.help: A 1960s rock kit, synthesized: a muffled bass drum with a felt beater, a loose snare, thin trashy hi-hats, washy cymbals and ringing toms, as in a small studio room of the time.
ui.drums.pattern.beat60s.help: A mid-sixties beat-group groove on the 1960s kit: bass drum on one and three with a push, backbeat snare, ride cymbal in eighths and a tambourine.
ui.drums.pattern.motown.help: The snare on every beat with a tambourine on two and four, on the 1960s kit.

ui.compare.fuxBetter.variety: You repeat the previous note here; Fux moves on. Repetition is the cheapest way out of a bad progression, and Aloysius praises avoiding it for variety's sake (1725 p. 74).
ui.compare.playerBetter.variety: Fux repeats his previous note here and you move on, which gives your line more variety.

ui.trio3.intro: Composition in three parts is the most perfect of all: in it the harmonic triad can be had complete, without the help of any further part.
ui.trio3.introLa: Tricinii Compositionem omnium perfectissimam esse, vel ex eo constat, quòd in illa sinè adjumento alterius partis perfecta harmoniae Trias haberi possit.

Pinch or Ctrl + wheel to zoom.

ui.continuo.preset.theorbo.help: Theorbo (plucked, chords rolled, the bass in its long strings) with a bass viol sustaining the bass

ui.continuo.preset.sostenuto.help: Recorded strings held with long bows: violins, violas, cellos and basses
ui.continuo.preset.brass.help: A recorded brass choir: trumpet on top, horns inside, trombones below and on the bass
ui.continuo.preset.analogPads.help: A vintage analog synthesizer: a pad that swells in slowly for the chords, a mono synth bass
ui.continuo.preset.rockBand.help: A 1960s-70s rock band, recorded: a clean lead guitar through a tape echo on the top note, a rhythm guitar strumming quarters, a bright picked bass

ui.trio3.intro2: Here recall and observe what we prescribed for this species in two voices, and what we said of the harmonic triad for semibreve against semibreve in three; with this relaxation, that in this species of three voices, for the sake of the harmonic triad, a minim may sometimes save two fifths by the leap of a third.

ui.trio3.cite2: Gradus ad Parnassum (1725), p. 94, translated in this game
ui.trio3.help2: One voice moves in minims, two to a bar, after a half rest; the other two in semibreves. At the close the upbeat may be tied into the penultimate bar (write the same note on both sides of the bar line), as Fux does in six of his nine examples (p. 96).

ui.trio3.intro3: Since the same order of proceeding is set for us in three-part composition as we used in the lessons for two parts, this lesson is plainly the composition of four crotchets against a semibreve; with this distinction, that as in two voices the crotchets had to agree with the semibreve of one part only, so here they must agree with the semibreves of two parts.
ui.trio3.introLa3: Cùm idem progrediendi ordo in hac Tricinii Compositione nobis propositus sit, quo in dandis Bicinii Lectionibus usi sumus, per se patet, hanc Lectionem esse Compositionem, quatuor Semiminimis contra Semibrevem positis constantem; cum hac tamen differentiali observatione, ut quemadmodum Semiminimae in Bicinii compositione cum unius duntaxat partis Semibrevi, ità in hac Tricinii compositione cum duarum partium Semibrevibus consonare debeant.
ui.trio3.cite3: Gradus ad Parnassum (1725), p. 99, translated in this game
ui.trio3.help3: One voice moves in crotchets, four to a bar; the other two in semibreves. Tap a quarter of the bar to write that crotchet; ← → move by one crotchet; R writes a rest. Fux opens one of his four with a crotchet rest. 'If the first crotchet cannot make the harmonic triad, see that the second or the third does' (p. 100).
ui.trio3.intro4: Here recall what was said of ligatures in two voices: the way of making them is hardly to be changed in three, but to be observed to the letter. It remains only to teach how the concord of the third part is to be added. Remember too what was said above: that a ligature is nothing but the retardation of the following note. Hence the paradox: the third part must be given the same concord it would have needed had the ligature been left out.
ui.trio3.introLa4: Hîc in mentem revocanda sunt, quae de Ligaturis in Bicinio dicta sunt, quarum efficiendi ratio in Tricinio minimè mutanda, sed ad amussim observanda est. Ad rem pertinebit modò docere, quemadmodum accedente parte tertiâ socialis illius concordantia instituenda sit. Refert quoque hîc meminisse, quod suprà dictum est; Ligaturam nempe aliud non esse, quàm retardationem Notae sequentis. Unde Paradoxum fit: eandem tertiae parti tribui oportere concordantiam, quae omissâ Ligaturâ adhibenda fuisset.
ui.trio3.cite4: Gradus ad Parnassum (1725), p. 103, translated in this game
ui.trio3.help4: One voice moves in ligatures: an upbeat tied over the bar line (write the same note on both sides), after a half rest; the other two in semibreves. Tap the left or right half of a bar; R writes a rest where no ligature can be made (pp. 108, 111). Over a held bass, ligatures of dissonances alone are elegant (p. 107); in the bass, a ligature may resolve into the fifth (pp. 105-106).

Where Bach figurates a chord (the C major prelude) the reading is close to the textbooks'; where the voices move independently, passing and suspended notes can be read as chord tones, a seventh where there is none, a chord a beat late. ui.wtc.intro.answer: The subject is Bach's; the answer is yours. Write the comes, the subject again a fifth higher or a fourth lower, in the subject's rhythm (the grey notes). Where the subject touches the dominant at its head, Bach's answer is tonal: the dominant is answered by the tonic (or the tonic by the dominant), so that the answer does not leave the key. Elsewhere the answer is real, a plain transposition.
ui.wtc.how.answer: Tap a grey note or move with ← →, and type its letter (A–G): the key signature is applied, and the note lands nearest the one before. ↑ ↓ move it a step (Shift: an octave); # and - alter it, n restores the natural; a tap on the staff places the note under the pointer. Space plays, Enter evaluates. The whole answer may stand an octave higher or lower.
ui.wtc.intro.counter: While the answer enters, the subject's voice goes on: the countersubject. Write that line, in Bach's rhythm, against Bach's answer. The species' doctrine of consonance and dissonance holds, carried into free rhythm and into the key; then set your line beside Bach's.
ui.wtc.how.counter: The keys are those of the answer. A dissonance stands as a passing note or neighbour, as a suspension (held or repeated, resolving down by step), as Fux's cambiata, against the answer's own passing note or suspension, or, off the beat, as a note entered or left by step or belonging to the harmony the two voices imply. Never two fifths or two octaves in a row.
ui.wtc.intro.study: Bach's exposition as he wrote it: the subject (dux), the answer (comes) with its mutations marked ✱, and what the dux sings against the answer. Listen in a well temperament: each key sounds as itself.

ui.wtc.keysHow: The fugues come from 21 of the 24 keys, from both books; C minor, E♭ minor and E minor have none in the dataset yet.
ui.wtc.bridge: Everything the species taught carries over: the consonances and their kinds, the dissonance that passes by step or is prepared and resolved, the ban on fifths and octaves in a row. What changes is the ground. The six modes become the twenty-four keys; the semibreve becomes Bach's rhythm; the cantus firmus becomes a subject that each voice takes up in turn. Fux himself goes on, after the species, to imitation and fugue. The answer at the fifth, kept inside the key by a mutation where the subject touches the dominant, is where the two worlds meet: the octave of the key divided, as Fux divides the octave of the mode, into a fifth and a fourth.
ui.wtc.temperaments: Werckmeister III (1691), Kirnberger III (1779) and Vallotti's temperament (18th century) are circulating: every key can be played, each with its own colour, the keys near C purer than the remote ones. Which temperament Bach meant by 'wohltemperirt' is disputed; equal temperament is offered for comparison.
ui.trio3.intro5: What this species is, and of what kind, I suppose is plain to you from what we said of it in two voices: a composition of all five species, ordered by a beautiful and elegant manner of singing. How the concords of the other two parts, made of semibreves, are to be set, I hardly doubt you already know from the three-voice exercises worked through so far; so that I think it superfluous to linger here explaining them further. Let us therefore go on to the examples without delay.
ui.trio3.introLa5: Quid, & qualis haec species sit, ex iis, quae de ea in Bicinio diximus, constare tibi suppono: esse nempè Compositionem omnium quinque specierum, pulchrâ concinnaque canendi ratione ordinatam. Quomodo autem reliquarum duarum partium semibrevibus constantium, instituendae sint concordantiae, ex Tricinii exercitationibus hucusque ventilatis tibi jam innotescere minimè dubito: adeò ut his ulteriùs explicandis hîc immorari supervacaneum existimem. Unde sinè mora ad exempla procedamus.
ui.trio3.cite5: Gradus ad Parnassum (1725), pp. 111-112, translated in this game
ui.trio3.help5: One voice is florid, the other two in semibreves. Choose a value (keys 8, 4, 3, 2, 6, 1: quaver to whole bar) and write: the note lasts that long. Hold (T) carries the previous note on, over the bar line as a ligature; R writes a rest. The florid line keeps the rules of two voices against the bass, and the bar's opening sonority those of three-voice first species. Fux's counsel (p. 114): oblique motion in every bar, as much as possible, makes the labour much easier.

tutor.rule.fos.no-repetition: In this species each upbeat brings a new note, which is then tied over the bar line; striking the downbeat's note again on its own upbeat is a whole note in disguise.
tutor.rule.fis.florid: Florid counterpoint is a garden of figures: mix the values of the earlier species. A line that barely moves (whole notes, or bars where nothing happens more than twice) is not this species.
tutor.rule.ts.no-repetition: Four crotchets against each whole note means four notes in motion: never strike the same note twice in a row.
tutor.rule.ss.no-repetition: Two minims against each whole note means two different notes: striking the same note twice is a whole note in disguise.

tutor.rule.fs.vertical-consonance: Every interval between the two voices must be a consonance (a unison, third, fifth, sixth or octave). This one is a dissonance.
tutor.rule.fs.opening-perfect: Begin on a perfect consonance. With your line below the cantus it must be the octave or the unison: a fifth below would put the lowest note outside the mode.
tutor.rule.fs.final-octave-or-unison: End on the octave or the unison.
tutor.rule.fs.cadence: The bar before the last prepares the ending: a major sixth when the cantus is below, a minor third when it is above, opening out to the octave or closing to the unison.
tutor.rule.fs.perfect-approach: Reach a perfect consonance (unison, fifth, octave) only by contrary or oblique motion. Here both voices move the same way into it, which makes parallel or hidden fifths or octaves.
tutor.rule.fs.unison-only-at-ends: The unison belongs only to the first and the last bar.
tutor.rule.fs.melodic-tritone: Never leap a tritone (an augmented fourth, as F up to B): 'mi contra fa'.
tutor.rule.fs.converging-leap-into-octave: Do not leap into an octave or unison from a wider interval with the voices closing in on each other.
tutor.rule.fs.unison-leap: Do not leap into or out of a unison.
tutor.rule.fs.prefer-contrary-motion: Use contrary or oblique motion as much as you can; here the voices move the same way more often than not.
tutor.rule.fs.prefer-imperfect-consonances: Too many perfect consonances: use more thirds and sixths than unisons, fifths and octaves between the first and the last bar.
tutor.rule.ss.downbeat-consonance: The note on the downbeat must always be a consonance.
tutor.rule.ss.passing-dissonance: A dissonance on the upbeat is allowed only as a passing note: reached by step and left by step in the same direction, filling a third.
tutor.rule.ss.cadence: In the bar before the last: a fifth on the downbeat, then a major sixth (cantus below) or a minor third (cantus above) on the upbeat.
tutor.rule.ss.downbeat-succession: Fifths (or octaves) on two downbeats in a row are not hidden by a short upbeat note in between; only a leap of a fourth or more in between would hide them.
tutor.rule.ts.downbeat-consonance: The first of the four quarters, on the downbeat, must be consonant.
tutor.rule.ts.dissonance: A dissonant quarter must pass by step, continuing in the same direction; or, on the second quarter, it may be the cambiata: reached by a step down and left by a skip of a third down to a consonance.
tutor.rule.ts.cadence: In the next-to-last bar the last quarter must lead into the final: a major sixth above the cantus (cantus below), a minor third below it (cantus above).
tutor.rule.fos.arsis-consonant: The first note of a ligature, on the upbeat, must always be consonant.
tutor.rule.fos.resolution: A dissonance on the downbeat must be tied over from the upbeat and resolve by step down to a consonance.
tutor.rule.fos.ligature-kinds: This ligature is not allowed: from the unison to the second, or from the octave to the ninth, it hides two unisons or octaves (cantus below); the seventh resolving to the octave is avoided (cantus above).
tutor.rule.fos.cadence: In the next-to-last bar: the seventh tied over and resolving to the major sixth (cantus below), or the second resolving to the minor third (cantus above).
tutor.rule.fos.ligature-where-possible: Tie the upbeat over into the next bar wherever you can. Plain minims are fine where no ligature fits; leaving out one that fits is allowed only as often as Fux does it in this exercise.
tutor.rule.fis.downbeat-consonance: A note struck on the downbeat must be consonant; only a note tied over the bar line may be dissonant there.
tutor.rule.fis.suspension: This tied dissonance is not handled as Fux handles it: it must be prepared by a consonance and resolve a step down to a consonance, at once or on the half bar after consonant notes (and, cantus below, never unison to second or octave to ninth; cantus above, never seventh to octave).
tutor.rule.fis.weak-dissonance: A dissonance off the downbeat must pass by step in one direction, be the cambiata, or step to a neighbour and back (a quaver, or a crotchet on the second or fourth crotchet).
tutor.rule.fis.quavers: Quavers come two at a time, on the second or the fourth crotchet of the bar, never on the first or third.
tutor.rule.fis.ligature: A note is tied over the bar line only from the second half of the bar: the first note of a ligature is on the upbeat.
tutor.rule.fis.cadence: The next-to-last bar must end on the note below the final: the major sixth (cantus below) or the minor third (cantus above).
tutor.rule.fis.limping: Two crotchets at the start of the bar with no ligature after them make the melody limp, says Aloysius: tie them into a ligature, or go on with two more crotchets. Advice, not a precept.
tutor.rule.t2.repeated: Never two minims on the same note (p. 96); only at the close may the upbeat be tied into the penultimate bar, where two separate minims would give a faulty unison or an empty octave.
tutor.rule.t2.downbeat-succession: Fifths (or octaves) on two downbeats in a row, with only a step between them on the upbeat. In three voices a leap of a third on the upbeat is enough to save them, 'for the sake of the harmonic triad' (pp. 94-95).
tutor.rule.t3.triad: In this bar no crotchet makes the harmonic triad with the two semibreves: 'if the first crotchet cannot make it, see that the second or the third does' (p. 100).
tutor.rule.t4.hidden-perfect: This ligature hides two fifths (or octaves): it is prepared and resolved on the same perfect consonance with another voice. 'As the ligature cannot prevent two faulty octaves, so it cannot save two fifths' (p. 105); in the lower part it is tolerated.

hints.rule.fos.no-repetition: In this species each upbeat brings a new note, which is then tied over the bar line; striking the downbeat's note again on its own upbeat is a whole note in disguise.
hints.rule.fis.florid: Florid counterpoint is a garden of figures: mix the values of the earlier species. A line that barely moves (whole notes, or bars where nothing happens more than twice) is not this species.
hints.rule.ts.no-repetition: Four crotchets against each whole note means four notes in motion: never strike the same note twice in a row.
hints.rule.ss.no-repetition: Two minims against each whole note means two different notes: striking the same note twice is a whole note in disguise.
hints.rules: Rules (breaking one means the exercise is not cleared)
hints.cadencePlain: Bar {bar}: no accidental is needed for the cadence in this mode.
hints.cadenceAltered: Bar {bar}: the cadence needs an accidental in this mode.
hints.rule.t1.consonance-bass: Against the bass (the lowest note of the bar) every voice must make a consonance: a third, fifth, sixth or octave, or their compounds. The fourth above the bass is a dissonance.
hints.rule.t1.upper-dissonance: The two upper voices must not make a second or a seventh with each other (a fourth between them is fine: it is the inside of a six-three).
hints.rule.t1.parallel-perfect: No two fifths or two octaves (or unisons) in a row between any two voices, not only against the bass.
hints.rule.t1.opening: Begin with the final of the mode (its home note: D in the D mode) as the lowest note of the first bar.
hints.rule.t1.final-chord: End on the final in the bass, with the octave, the fifth or the major third above it, never the minor third.
hints.rule.t1.cadence: The cadence: one voice must reach the final by a semitone (the raised seventh rising; in E, the F falling).
hints.rule.t1.melodic: In your voices: no augmented leap, no major sixth, no seventh.
hints.rule.t1.direct-perfect: A fifth or octave reached by similar motion is tolerated in three voices when the upper of the two voices moves by step; here it leaps. A curiosity: Fux himself does exactly this once, in Fux #116 (bars 6–7, his top voice leaping C–A into a twelfth over the bass), and says nothing about it.
hints.rule.t1.false-fifth: Avoid reaching a diminished fifth by similar motion.
hints.rule.t1.triad: Aim for the full triad, a third and a fifth above the bass; this bar has only perfect consonances over the bass.
hints.rule.t1.unison: Avoid unisons between voices except at the beginning and the end: the octave serves the harmony better.
hints.rule.fs.vertical-consonance: Every vertical interval must be a consonance: unison, third, fifth, sixth or octave (or a compound of these). The fourth counts as a dissonance.
hints.rule.fs.prefer-contrary-motion: Use contrary or oblique motion as much as possible.
hints.rule.fs.perfect-approach: Reach a perfect consonance (unison, fifth, octave) only by contrary or oblique motion, never by parallel or similar motion.
hints.rule.fs.opening-perfect: Begin on a perfect consonance. With the counterpoint below the cantus, begin on the octave or unison, not the fifth, to stay in the mode.
hints.rule.fs.final-octave-or-unison: End on the octave or the unison.
hints.rule.fs.cadence: In the next-to-last bar: a major sixth when the cantus is below, a minor third when the cantus is above; then the octave or unison.
hints.rule.fs.unison-only-at-ends: Use the unison only in the first and the last bar.
hints.rule.fs.converging-leap-into-octave: Do not leap into an octave or unison from a more distant consonance with the voices converging.
hints.rule.fs.unison-leap: Do not leap out of a unison, or into one.
hints.glance.compounds: Compound intervals above the octave count as their simple form.
hints.glance.startBelow: begin on a unison, fifth or octave above the cantus
hints.glance.startAbove: begin on a unison or the octave below the cantus
hints.glance.end: end on the octave or the unison
hints.glance.parallelBan: Parallel fifths and octaves: the most strictly forbidden progression.
hints.def.perfect: Perfect consonances: the unison, the fifth and the octave. They sound complete and stable, so the rules limit how they may be approached.
hints.def.imperfect: Imperfect consonances: thirds and sixths, major or minor. They sound sweet but not final, and may be approached by any motion.
hints.def.dissonance: Dissonances: seconds, fourths, the tritone and sevenths. In first species every vertical interval must be a consonance, so none of these may appear.
hints.def.unison: Unison (1): both voices sing the same pitch.
hints.def.fifth: Perfect fifth (5): seven semitones, e.g. C up to G.
hints.def.octave: Octave (8): the same note twelve semitones higher, e.g. C to the next C.
hints.def.m3: Minor third: three semitones, e.g. A up to C.
hints.def.M3: Major third: four semitones, e.g. C up to E.
hints.def.m6: Minor sixth: eight semitones, e.g. E up to C.
hints.def.M6: Major sixth: nine semitones, e.g. C up to A.
hints.def.second: Seconds: neighbouring notes (one or two semitones apart). Dissonant.
hints.def.fourth: Perfect fourth: five semitones (C up to F). Against the lowest voice it counts as a dissonance in this style (between two upper voices it is fine). If you find it surprising that so simple and smooth an interval should be 'dissonant' — the Greeks counted it among the consonances — you are onto something theorists have argued about for centuries.
hints.def.tritone: Tritone: three whole tones, six semitones (the augmented fourth F up to B, or the diminished fifth B up to F). Dissonant. Fux calls it 'mi contra fa': in the old solmization a melody was sung on overlapping six-note scales (hexachords), and B was sung as 'mi' while F was 'fa', so a 'mi' set against a 'fa' made exactly this interval — 'mi contra fa est diabolus in musica', as the old saying Fux quotes has it. Hence its other name: the devil's interval.
hints.def.seventh: Sevenths: ten semitones (minor) or eleven (major). Dissonant in this style: they lean towards a resolution, usually a step down. To modern ears a seventh hardly sounds harsh — sevenths colour chords everywhere from the blues and jazz to soul and pop — but Fux's measure is the pure sound of voices in consonance, and against that a seventh still pulls.
hints.def.compound: A compound interval is wider than an octave; it behaves like its simple form an octave smaller (a tenth like a third, a twelfth like a fifth).
hints.def.parallel: Parallel motion: both voices move in the same direction and keep the same interval (e.g. fifth to fifth). Into a perfect consonance it is forbidden.
hints.def.similar: Similar motion: both voices move in the same direction but by different amounts, so the interval changes. Into a perfect consonance it is forbidden.
hints.def.oblique: Oblique motion: one voice holds its note while the other moves.
hints.def.contrary: Contrary motion: the voices move in opposite directions. Fux recommends it as much as possible.
hints.rule.fs.prefer-imperfect-consonances: Use more imperfect consonances (thirds, sixths) than perfect ones (unisons, fifths, octaves) between the first and the last bar.
hints.glance.dissonant2: Dissonances (only on the upbeat, passing by step)
hints.def.dissonance2: Dissonances: seconds, fourths, the tritone and sevenths. In second species the downbeat note is always consonant; the upbeat note may be dissonant only when it passes by step from the note before to the note after, filling a third.
hints.glance.dissonant3: Dissonances (off the downbeat: passing by step, or the cambiata)
hints.def.dissonance3: Dissonances: seconds, fourths, the tritone and sevenths. In third species the first quarter is always consonant; another quarter may be dissonant when it passes by step in one direction, or as the cambiata: the second quarter, reached by a step down and left by a skip of a third down to a consonance.
hints.glance.dissonant4: Dissonances (on the downbeat, tied over and resolved down by step)
hints.def.dissonance4: Dissonances: seconds, fourths, the tritone and sevenths. In fourth species the dissonance comes on the downbeat, tied over from a consonant upbeat, and resolves by step down to a consonance on the next upbeat.
hints.glance.dissonant5: Dissonances (tied over the bar line and resolved down; or passing, cambiata, neighbour)
hints.def.dissonance5: Dissonances: seconds, fourths, the tritone and sevenths. In florid counterpoint each value keeps its species' treatment: on the downbeat only tied over and resolved a step down (the resolution may be decorated); elsewhere passing by step, the cambiata, or a quick neighbour and back.
hints.device.rest: A half rest may take the place of the first note.
hints.device.leap: When the voices are so close that contrary motion is impossible, a leap of a minor sixth or of an octave (p. 60) opens the space again.

hints.lookAhead: Decide the ending before you begin, and look one or two bars ahead while writing.

help.howto: You are Josephus, Fux's pupil. Against each cantus firmus — the given melody in whole notes — write a line of your own that obeys the rules of the species, then press Evaluate. Aloysius marks what breaks a rule; a clean result earns the star and opens Fux's own solution, to see, hear and compare. Point at anything on the screen to read what it does in the bar at the foot.
help.mouse: Mouse: click your staff to write; click a note and drag it to move it; click below or above the staves to select a bar. Ctrl + wheel (or a trackpad pinch) makes the notes larger or smaller, as do − and + above the score. On a phone or tablet: tap your staff to write, tap above or below the staves to select, swipe to scroll, pinch to make the notes larger or smaller; the score stays on one line and scrolls sideways.

help.keys.step: Move the note up / down a step; right after a letter, the note just written. With Shift: an octave
help.keys.letter: Write that note, in the octave nearest the last one, and move on to the next
help.keys.rest: Rest (the first half of second and fourth species)
help.keys.tie: Repeat the previous note; in fourth species, the tie over the bar line; in fifth species, hold the note on (over the bar line, the tie)

help.keys.value: Fifth species: the value written next: quaver, crotchet, dotted crotchet, minim, dotted minim, whole bar

gloss.gradus: Gradus ad Parnassum ('Steps to Parnassus', Vienna 1725): Johann Joseph Fux's textbook of counterpoint, written in Latin as a dialogue between a master, Aloysius, and his pupil, Josephus. The exercises of this game are its exercises.
gloss.aloysius: Aloysius: the master in Fux's dialogue, standing for Palestrina (Giovanni Pierluigi da Palestrina) — Aloysius is the Latin form of Luigi. He speaks for Fux.
gloss.josephus: Josephus: the pupil in Fux's dialogue (Fux's own first name, Joseph). In this game, Josephus is you.
gloss.cantusFirmus: Cantus firmus ('fixed song'): the given melody, in whole notes, which you write against. It never changes.
gloss.counterpoint: Counterpoint (contrapunctus, 'note against note'): a line written against another so that both make sense at once — each a good melody, together a good harmony.
gloss.species: Species: Fux's five steps of rhythm. First: one note against each whole note. Second: two. Third: four. Fourth: notes tied over the bar line (syncopations). Fifth: florid, all of these mixed.
gloss.final: The final: the home note of a mode, on which its melodies end (D in the D mode, E in the E mode ...). It is the nearest thing in the old modes to what we call the tonic; the cantus firmus always begins and ends on it.
gloss.mode: Mode: the old scales of church music, each named by its final (Fux's are on D, E, F, G, A and C, with only white keys). Each has its own colour: the D mode sounds like a minor scale with a raised sixth, the F mode like a major scale with a raised fourth, and so on.
gloss.interval: Interval: the distance between two notes, counted in letter names, both ends included: C–E is a third (C, D, E), C–G a fifth. Sung together it is a harmonic interval; one after the other, a melodic interval.
gloss.consonance: Consonance: an interval that sounds at rest — unison, third, fifth, sixth, octave (and the same an octave or more higher).
gloss.perfect: Perfect consonances: the unison, fifth and octave. Complete and stable, so the rules limit how they may be reached.
gloss.imperfect: Imperfect consonances: thirds and sixths, major or minor. Sweet but not final; reached freely.
gloss.dissonance: Dissonance: an interval that sounds in tension and wants to move — seconds, fourths (against the lowest voice), the tritone, sevenths.
gloss.motion: Motion: how two voices move from one sonority to the next — contrary (opposite ways), oblique (one stays), similar (same way, different distances) or parallel (same way, same interval).
gloss.cadence: Cadence: the formula that ends a piece. In Fux's counterpoint the voices close onto the final by step from opposite sides, one of them by a semitone (the leading tone).
gloss.leadingTone: Leading tone: the note a semitone below the final, rising into it at the cadence. In the modes it often needs a sharp (C♯ in D, F♯ in G, G♯ in A); the E mode instead falls onto its final from F, a semitone above.
gloss.downbeat: Downbeat and upbeat (thesis and arsis): the first and second half of the bar. The downbeat is the strong part; most rules about consonance are about it.
gloss.passing: Passing note: a note between two others a third apart, filling the gap by step. On a weak beat it may be dissonant.
gloss.cambiata: Cambiata ('exchanged note'): a dissonance reached by a step down and left by a leap of a third down, then a step up — a figure Fux allows in third species.
gloss.ligature: Ligature: a note tied over the bar line (fourth species). If it becomes dissonant against the new bass note, it is a suspension.
gloss.suspension: Suspension: a note held over the bar line that clashes with the next note of the cantus and must then resolve, a step down, to a consonance.
gloss.miContraFa: Mi contra fa: the tritone. In the old solmization B was sung 'mi' and F 'fa'; a mi set against a fa made the tritone — 'diabolus in musica'.
gloss.ficta: Musica ficta ('feigned music'): accidentals the singers added to the written notes, chiefly to avoid the tritone and to sharpen leading tones at cadences. Fux writes them out — his B♭s and sharps are of this kind, not part of the mode itself.
gloss.triad: Triad: a chord of a note with its third and fifth above. In three voices Fux wants the complete triad in every bar unless some reason forbids it.
gloss.sixThree: Six-three: a chord with a third and a sixth above the bass (the inside interval between the upper voices is a fourth, which is fine there).
gloss.figures: Figures (figured bass): small numbers under a bass note telling a keyboard player which intervals to play above it — 6 for a sixth, 5/3 (or nothing) for a triad, and so on.
gloss.continuo: Basso continuo: the keyboard (or lute, or theorbo) accompaniment of Baroque music, improvised over a bass line from its figures. Here it is generated for pleasure and plays no part in the judging.
gloss.versions: Versions of your line: its inversion (upside down), retrograde (backwards), retrograde inversion (both) and a canon (your line again, a few beats later) — the devices of learned counterpoint. Switch them on with Advanced (⚙).

guide.gradus.help: What Fux's Gradus ad Parnassum is, and why it is still used
guide.gradus.quote: I will not be deterred by the most passionate haters of study, nor by the depravity of the present time.
guide.gradus.quoteCite: Fux, preface to the reader (1725), in English translation; the Latin is not among our scans and has not been checked
guide.gradus.p1: Johann Joseph Fux (c. 1660–1741), court Kapellmeister in Vienna, published Gradus ad Parnassum in 1725, in Latin, dedicated to the Emperor Charles VI. The title means 'steps to Parnassus' — the mountain of the Muses — and the book climbs it one step at a time.
guide.gradus.p2: Its practical part is a dialogue. Aloysius, the master (he stands for Palestrina, whose name Pierluigi gives Aloysius in Latin), teaches Josephus, the pupil, to write counterpoint against a given melody: first in two voices, then in three and four, each through five species of rhythm, from note against note to the florid. Josephus tries, makes mistakes, is corrected, and asks why. In this game Josephus is you, and the exercises, the cantus firmi and the solutions are Fux's own.
guide.gradus.p3: The book became the standard method for two centuries. Leopold Mozart is said to have taught his son Wolfgang from it; J. S. Bach and Beethoven held it in high esteem; Haydn worked through every one of its exercises. Lorenz Mizler translated it into German in 1742, and in the following decades it appeared in Italian, French and English. In Alfred Mann's English translation it is still used to teach counterpoint today.
guide.gradus.ref: Alfred Mann (tr. and ed.), The Study of Counterpoint from Johann Joseph Fux's Gradus ad Parnassum (New York: Norton, 1943; revised 1965).
guide.gradus.p4: Why Fux, and not simply the rules? Because he teaches the way a composer learns: by writing, being stopped, and understanding the reason. The rules in this game are his, read from the 1725 print, with the page beside each; where we had to interpret him, we say so.

tips.freedom: By the main rules there are {n} correct lines for this cantus: room enough to make one your own.

tips.leapUp: Between bars {bar} and {next} the cantus leaps up a {size}: answer with a step down (contrary motion), and stay clear of fifths and octaves there.
tips.leapDown: Between bars {bar} and {next} the cantus leaps down a {size}: answer with a step up (contrary motion), and stay clear of fifths and octaves there.
tips.peak: The cantus reaches its highest note, {note}, in bar {bar}: your line, above it, will be pressed together there; keep a third or a sixth in hand.
tips.low: The cantus reaches its lowest note, {note}, in bar {bar}: your line, below it, will be pressed down there; keep a third or a sixth in hand.
tips.tritone: Bars {bars}: against the cantus's {note}, the {avoid} makes a tritone or a diminished fifth. Leave it out there.
tips.method: How these are found: the game tries every line under the main rules of the species (in second species bar by bar over the downbeats, with every upbeat between them), with the notes Fux uses (naturals, B♭, and the sharps of the cadence in the last four bars), and counts those that get through. Fux's own solutions are among them. The evaluation still applies every rule.

quick.step1: The lower or upper staff holds the cantus firmus, the given melody in whole notes. Write your own line on the other staff: click where a note should go (or use the arrow keys and the letters A–G).
quick.step2: Each pair of notes sounding together makes an interval, written between the staves. The chart below sorts the intervals into perfect consonances, imperfect consonances and dissonances, and the rules say how they may follow one another; press ▶ beside a rule to watch it broken and then kept.
quick.step3: Press Play to hear both lines, then Evaluate. Aloysius marks what breaks a rule; a line with no rule broken earns the ★ (a gold 🌟 with no advice broken either) and opens Fux's own solution to compare.
